hero.headline: Rubio testifies on U.S. demands in Iran peace talks as conflict worsens
hero.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio appeared before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Tuesday to detail U.S. demands in ongoing negotiations with Iran, marking his first public testimony since the Trump administration launched the war in February. His appearance comes as Iran has announced it is halting peace talks and moving to fully close the Strait of Hormuz, intensifying the regional conflict.

Rubio claimed that Iran has agreed to negotiate aspects of its nuclear program that officials refused to discuss a month earlier. "There is the prospect before us, which could happen today, it could happen tomorrow, it could happen next week - that for the first time, certainly in my memory, they have agreed to negotiate aspects of their nuclear program that just a month ago they said they would not," he told senators.

The secretary's optimism contrasts sharply with Iran's announcement that it would stop exchanging messages with Washington through intermediaries, citing Israel's military operations in Lebanon as a ceasefire violation. President Trump later insisted that conversations "have been going on continuously" and denied reports that officials had stopped speaking.

Rubio outlined a two-phase framework for negotiations. He stated that reopening the Strait of Hormuz serves as a precondition for talks, not a bargaining chip. Iran must declare it is not charging tolls, assist in removing mines it placed there, and commit not to fire on ships. Only after these conditions are met would phase two discussions begin, which would require Iran to dispose of its highly enriched uranium stockpile and accept "severe and long-term limitations, or cancellation of enrichment activity."

When questioned by Democratic Senator Chris Murphy about offering sanctions relief to reopen the waterway, Rubio ruled out that approach. "Any sanctions relief is condition-based," he said, tied to Iran's nuclear program. "That's not been discussed, that's not been offered."

Regarding Iran's military capabilities, Rubio suggested that the country's missile program has been "substantially degraded" and its drone-building capability "eroded." He claimed there is "no Iranian navy," stating it "lies at the bottom of the ocean." However, he acknowledged that Iran still possesses "a lot of drones" because they are relatively easy to manufacture.

These claims about Iran's military destruction have been contested by independent analysis. The New York Times reported in May that Iran retained roughly 70 percent of its prewar missile stockpile, though over 85 percent of its ballistic missile, drone and naval defense industrial base has been damaged or destroyed.

Rubio noted that a U.S. counter-blockade targeting all ships seeking Iranian ports is costing Tehran "hundreds of millions of dollars a day" in lost oil revenue. This blockade followed Iran's failure to honor an April ceasefire agreement that included a commitment to reopen the strait.

cards.headline: Trump confronted Netanyahu over threat to resume Beirut strikes
cards.teaser: The president raised his voice and used profanity during a call about Israeli military operations in Lebanon.
cards.body:
President Trump angrily confronted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over Israel's threats to resume airstrikes on Beirut's southern suburbs during a phone call on Monday. According to reports, Trump used profanity during the exchange, demanding to know what Netanyahu was doing.

Following the confrontation, Israel halted strikes on Beirut, though it continues military operations in southern Lebanon. The call came after Iran indicated it would suspend talks with the US over Israel's campaign in Lebanon.

cards.headline: Russian strikes on Kyiv kill at least 22 across Ukraine
cards.body:
Russian forces launched a massive overnight assault on Ukrainian cities using hundreds of drones and dozens of missiles, killing at least 22 people and leaving others trapped under collapsed buildings.

The attack targeted five major cities: Kyiv, Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Poltava, and Kharkiv. According to Ukraine's air force, Russia deployed 73 missiles and 656 drones, including eight hypersonic Tsirkon missiles. The strikes hit residential buildings, energy infrastructure, and businesses across multiple locations.

In Dnipro, five people were killed as Russian forces hit the city throughout the night, according to regional officials. Four bodies were discovered in the ruins of a destroyed house, with rescue workers continuing to search for additional victims in the rubble. At least 34 people were injured in the overnight strikes, which authorities said lasted for hours. Fires broke out across the city, partly destroying several apartment blocks and private residences.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the pattern of attacks on social media, stating: "The Russians' tactics have not changed: strike drones, cruise missiles and a significant amount of ballistics. Most of the targets are ordinary infrastructure in cities. Residential buildings, energy, and enterprises have been damaged."

In response to the escalating violence, Zelenskyy asked President Donald Trump to send Patriot missiles to Ukraine to help defend against future attacks.

Authorities reported that Ukrainian air defenses repelled the majority of the incoming drones, which represented one of the largest assault waves in several days. Additional casualties were reported in Odesa and Kharkiv, with at least three people injured in those cities.

The overnight assault followed a prisoner exchange between Russia and Ukraine on Friday, in which both sides swapped 193 service members. These exchanges were negotiated as part of US-brokered talks between Moscow and Kyiv, though negotiations have produced no progress on ending Russia's invasion.

Ukraine also conducted long-range drone strikes deep inside Russian territory. A woman was killed and a man seriously injured in a drone strike in the Russian border region of Belgorod.

The repeated strikes on Ukrainian cities come as Russia faces mounting battlefield losses and casualties in the conflict. Military analysts suggest Moscow is using intensified bombing campaigns as leverage for potential future negotiations, hoping to strengthen its position at the bargaining table. The combination of advance warnings about strikes and the subsequent delays before attacks appeared designed to create psychological pressure on Ukrainian civilians, observers said.

Rescue operations continued as workers searched through debris at multiple sites across the country, with the death toll expected to rise as recovery efforts proceeded.

cards.headline: Israel strikes southern Lebanon after holding off Beirut attack
cards.teaser: Israel continued military operations against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon after pressure from President Trump led Prime Minister Netanyahu to delay planned strikes on Beirut.
cards.body:
Israel has continued military operations in southern Lebanon while maintaining a partial truce in the capital region following a US-brokered deal. Prime Minister Netanyahu, responding to pressure from President Trump, refrained from attacking Beirut but reaffirmed Israel's commitment to its campaign against Hezbollah.

The restraint on Beirut strikes marks a shift in Israel's broader offensive, though southern Lebanon remains an active theater of operations. This escalation risks complicating ongoing peace negotiations involving Iran.

cards.headline: Trump appoints mortgage executive Bill Pulte as acting director of national intelligence
cards.body:
President Trump has named Bill Pulte, head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, as acting director of national intelligence. The appointment came days after Tulsi Gabbard announced her departure from the role.

Pulte, whose grandfather founded the PulteGroup homebuilder, previously had no government experience before Trump appointed him to lead the FHFA, which oversees the federal housing lenders Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. He will remain in his housing finance position while taking on the intelligence role temporarily as acting director, meaning he can serve without Senate confirmation.

The appointment has generated significant alarm among national security professionals and lawmakers. Critics have emphasized that Pulte lacks any background in national security or intelligence work, despite the position's critical importance in coordinating the work of agencies including the CIA, NSA, and FBI.

As head of the FHFA, Pulte has attracted scrutiny for using his authority to investigate Trump's political opponents. He has publicly accused targets of the president, including Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, of committing mortgage fraud. Cook has denied wrongdoing. A former high-ranking official described his handling of the Cook case as "very bizarre."

Democratic Senator Mark Warner, vice-chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, criticized the selection. "Rather than selecting a respected national security professional capable of delivering independent judgments, the president has chosen an official who has demonstrated not just willingness but eagerness to use the authorities of government to pursue political retribution," Warner said. He argued that Trump was "not looking for an intelligence leader who will follow the facts or speak truth to power, but rather someone who will be willing to shape intelligence around the president's wishes."

Even Senate Republicans expressed concerns about the appointment. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said "we don't need a weaponized" national intelligence director and indicated Pulte would face a "lengthy road ahead" if nominated for a permanent position requiring Senate confirmation. Thune stressed the need for "professionals" in the role rather than someone focused on political aims.

Other Republican senators on the intelligence committee voiced skepticism. Susan Collins said she did not know Pulte's background, while James Lankford stated he was unaware of any intelligence experience and emphasized that the role "should be a neutral."

Trump justified the appointment on Truth Social, saying Pulte has "deep experience managing the most sensitive matters in America."

The director of national intelligence position was created after the September 11 attacks to improve coordination among intelligence agencies. The role requires synthesizing intelligence reports across government and advising the president on classified national security threats. The position has traditionally been filled by individuals with extensive backgrounds in intelligence, military service, or national security policy.

cards.headline: Trump signs order seeking voluntary safety reviews of AI models before public release
cards.teaser: An executive order asks AI companies to voluntarily submit powerful models for government testing up to 30 days before release.
cards.body:
President Trump signed an executive order creating a voluntary framework for AI safety. Under the new guidelines, tech companies are asked to submit their most powerful models for government review up to 30 days before public release.

The administration says the voluntary approach will help improve national security and cybersecurity protections. This represents a shift from Trump's earlier deregulatory stance on AI, though his reluctance to impose mandatory requirements on the tech industry remains evident.

cards.headline: Two shot dead during Kenya protests over US Ebola center
cards.teaser: Two people were killed as protests erupted in Kenya against US plans to build an Ebola quarantine and treatment facility.
cards.body:
Two people were shot dead during protests in Kenya against a planned US Ebola quarantine centre. The proposed treatment facility has provoked strong opposition from local residents, who have demonstrated near the construction site.

The US project has generated significant public anger in the region, with protests intensifying as plans to establish the facility have progressed.

cards.headline: British couple loses appeal of Iran prison sentence
cards.teaser: Lindsay and Craig Foreman, a British couple arrested in Iran during a global motorbike trip, have lost their appeal against jail sentences.
cards.body:
A British couple has lost their appeal against prison sentences handed down by Iranian courts, according to their family. Lindsay and Craig Foreman were arrested in January 2025 while traveling through Iran during a global motorbike journey.

The couple's family confirmed the failed appeal. They had been detained for over a year before the court proceedings concluded with the rejection of their appeal against the original sentences.

cards.headline: Canada requests renewal of North American trade pact
cards.teaser: Canada formally asked the US and Mexico to renew the USMCA trade agreement as negotiations continue amid tensions.
cards.body:
Canada formally requested renewal of the North American free trade agreement through a letter from Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc to his counterparts in the US and Mexico. The minister called for the three countries to renew the USMCA trade deal.

The request comes as LeBlanc visits Washington for meetings with the US Trade Representative. Shortly before the scheduled trade talks, President Trump referred to Canada as the 51st state, repeating a characterization he has made on previous occasions.

cards.headline: Missing New Jersey congressman receives Trump endorsement
cards.teaser: Republican Congressman Tom Kean Jr, who has not been seen for months, received President Trump's endorsement ahead of an election he is expected to win.
cards.body:
Republican Congressman Tom Kean Jr. has been absent from public view for several months. Despite his prolonged disappearance, he is expected to win his election on Tuesday.

President Trump endorsed Kean ahead of the election, lending his support to the New Jersey congressman despite questions surrounding his extended absence from the public eye.

cards.headline: Stephen Curry signs deal with Chinese sneaker company Li-Ning
cards.teaser: The NBA star agreed to a partnership with Li-Ning that includes plans for sportswear, athleisure products, and stores across the US and China.
cards.body:
Stephen Curry has signed a 10-year endorsement deal with Chinese sneaker company Li-Ning. The agreement covers sportswear and athleisure products, with plans to open stores in both the United States and China. This partnership marks the end of Curry's free agency following his departure from Under Armour.

The deal represents another high-profile collaboration between an NBA star and a Chinese footwear brand, as Li-Ning continues to expand its presence in the American market through partnerships with prominent basketball players.

cards.headline: White House Correspondents Association reschedules annual dinner following shooting
cards.teaser: The dinner has been moved to July 24 after a shooting incident prompted cancellation of the original event.
cards.body:
The White House Correspondents Association announced it will hold its annual dinner on July 24 after rescheduling the event. The original dinner was disrupted by a shooting incident that forced organizers to cancel.

The association said it will increase security measures for the rescheduled event. The annual dinner traditionally brings together journalists, politicians, and celebrities in Washington. The July date gives organizers time to implement enhanced security protocols.

cards.headline: Primaries underway for California governor and multiple state races
cards.teaser: Voters cast ballots in California's gubernatorial race, the Los Angeles mayoral contest, and other state primary elections.
cards.body:
Primary elections are underway across six states today, including California, Iowa, Montana, New Jersey, South Dakota, and New Mexico. California voters are selecting the top two candidates to advance in the governor's race, while Los Angeles voters are choosing mayoral candidates.

The California gubernatorial primary and Los Angeles mayoral race have drawn national attention as significant tests for the Democratic Party. Results from these contests will determine which candidates advance to the general election.

cards.headline: Israel strikes southern Lebanon as partial Hezbollah ceasefire continues
cards.teaser: Israeli forces conducted operations in southern Lebanon but did not strike Beirut after a U.S.-announced agreement.
cards.body:
Israel has continued military operations in southern Lebanon while maintaining a partial truce with Hezbollah. Under a U.S.-brokered agreement, Israeli forces have ceased strikes on Beirut, though combat operations persist in the south.

The arrangement falls short of a comprehensive ceasefire, representing instead a limited reduction in hostilities between the two sides. The pause in strikes against the capital marks a significant shift in the conflict's scope.

cards.body:
A British couple imprisoned in Iran has lost their appeal, according to their family. Lindsay and Craig Foreman were arrested in January 2025 while traveling through Iran as part of a global motorcycle journey.

The couple's detention has now extended beyond a year as they pursued legal challenges to their sentences. Their family confirmed the appeal was unsuccessful.

hero.headline: Container ship struck by projectiles at Iraqi port
hero.teaser: A vessel owned by Mediterranean Shipping Company was hit by two projectiles at an Iraqi port, highlighting ongoing threats to maritime traffic.
hero.body:
A Mediterranean Shipping Company vessel was struck by two projectiles while at an Iraqi port. The attack occurred as negotiations between the United States and Iran continue over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

The incident underscores persistent risks to commercial shipping in the region despite diplomatic efforts. The strait remains a critical chokepoint for global maritime trade, and threats to vessels have continued even as talks progress between the two nations.

cards.headline: Seven states sue Trump administration over canceled wind farm
cards.teaser: Multiple states filed suit against the federal government after a deal paid a French company to abandon an offshore wind project.
cards.body:
Six US states have sued the Trump administration over its decision to cancel a major offshore wind lease off the coast of New York. In March, federal officials announced they would pay nearly $1 billion in taxpayer dollars to French energy firm TotalEnergies to terminate the company's plans for offshore windfarms off New York and North Carolina.

As part of the deal, TotalEnergies agreed to kill the projects and pledged not to develop any new offshore wind projects in the United States. The company also committed to investing hundreds of millions of dollars in oil and gas projects instead. State attorneys general argue the $1 billion settlement is unlawful.

cards.headline: Stock markets hit new records as tech shares rise
cards.teaser: The S&P 500 reached a fresh high as semiconductor and technology stocks led gains.
cards.body:
Major stock indexes climbed to record levels, with the S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average both reaching new peaks. Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Alphabet helped fuel the rally, driving momentum in artificial intelligence related investments.

Semiconductor stocks gained during the session, with Nvidia among the leaders pushing chip manufacturers higher. The strong performance capped a robust May for equity markets as investors continued to favor technology sector companies.

cards.headline: Blue Origin targets end of year for New Glenn rocket return
cards.teaser: The company pledged to fly its New Glenn rocket again before the year ends following an earlier explosion.
cards.body:
Blue Origin announced it plans to launch its New Glenn rocket again before the end of the year. CEO Dave Limp said the damage to the company's Florida launchpad from last week's explosion was less severe than initially feared. The company has not yet disclosed the cause of the incident.

Despite the setback, the Space Force has signed a new launch agreement with Blue Origin. NASA official Jared Isaacman previously stated that full restoration of the damaged launch pad could take until 2028.

cards.headline: Trump donor gave $5.5 million estate to Kennedy's anti-vaccine group
cards.teaser: A member of the Mellon family transferred a large Connecticut property to Children's Health Defense at no cost.
cards.body:
A Trump supporter from the Mellon family transferred a $5.5 million estate to Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s anti-vaccine organization last year. The donation consisted of adjacent Connecticut properties totaling approximately 300 acres.

Children's Health Defense received the land at no cost. The transfer represents a significant financial contribution to the organization led by Kennedy, who has promoted vaccine skepticism.

cards.headline: Stephen Curry signs deal with Chinese sneaker maker Li-Ning
cards.teaser: The NBA star reached an agreement with the Chinese company for sportswear and retail expansion in both countries.
cards.body:
Stephen Curry has signed a 10-year endorsement deal with Li-Ning, the Chinese sneaker company, concluding his free agency following his split from Under Armour.

The partnership extends beyond footwear to include sportswear and athleisure lines, with retail expansion planned for both the United States and China. The agreement reflects a growing trend of NBA players partnering with Chinese athletic brands.

cards.headline: Martin Scorsese backs AI image generation startup
cards.teaser: The filmmaker invested in Black Forest Labs, signaling Hollywood's changing stance on artificial intelligence technology.
cards.body:
Martin Scorsese is backing Black Forest Labs, an artificial intelligence startup that generates images and video. His support signals a significant shift in Hollywood's stance toward AI technology.

The acclaimed director's investment reflects growing acceptance of artificial intelligence tools within the film industry, marking a departure from earlier skepticism about the technology's role in creative work.

hero.headline: Hackers breach Dashlane password manager, steal customer vaults
hero.body:
Password management company Dashlane has disclosed that attackers gained unauthorized access to customer accounts and downloaded their password vaults. According to the company, hackers were able to circumvent its two-factor authentication system through brute-force attacks, granting them entry to customer data.

Dashlane serves millions of users who rely on the service to store sensitive information including login credentials and payment details within encrypted vaults. The company has not specified how many customers were affected by the breach.

Password managers function as centralized repositories for authentication information, making them attractive targets for cybercriminals. When a password manager is successfully compromised, it can expose all stored credentials at once. However, in this case, the vaults that attackers downloaded contain encrypted passwords rather than plaintext versions. This means the actual passwords remain protected by encryption, and their security depends on the strength of each user's master password.

The attack exploited Dashlane's two-factor authentication system through brute-force methods. Two-factor authentication adds a second verification layer beyond passwords, typically requiring users to provide additional confirmation such as a code transmitted to their phone or generated by an authenticator application. In brute-force attacks, perpetrators systematically test numerous possible combinations until discovering one that provides access.

Dashlane has not revealed specific details about the vulnerability that enabled the brute-force attack to succeed. The company also has not disclosed what actions it has implemented to prevent future similar incidents. Additionally, Dashlane has not announced whether it is directing affected customers to change their master passwords or implement other protective measures.

Customers whose vaults were downloaded face potential risk of password exposure if attackers can successfully crack the encryption protecting their master password. This represents a significant security concern because a compromised master password would unlock access to all stored credentials within a customer's vault.

The disclosure raises questions about the security practices at major password management providers and the effectiveness of their authentication systems. Password managers have become increasingly popular as tools for managing the growing number of online accounts that individuals must maintain, but breaches highlight the critical importance of choosing services with robust security measures.

Users affected by this breach should consider changing their master passwords and reviewing their accounts for any unauthorized activity. They may also want to monitor their financial accounts and credit reports for signs of fraud. For those concerned about their security, this incident underscores the importance of using strong, unique master passwords that would be difficult for attackers to crack through brute-force methods.

Dashlane and the affected customers remain in a situation where the full scope and impact of the breach continue to unfold as the company conducts its investigation.

cards.headline: Amazon sued over Ring doorbell facial recognition feature
cards.teaser: A class action lawsuit claims Ring stored images of people passing by cameras without their consent.
cards.body:
A Virginia resident named Charles Sigwalt filed a class action lawsuit against Amazon in Seattle, challenging the Ring doorbell's Familiar Faces feature. The lawsuit alleges that the feature captures and stores facial images of people passing by Ring cameras without their consent.

The Familiar Faces feature is designed to identify individuals recorded by Ring doorbell cameras. Sigwalt's lawsuit contends that this practice of collecting and retaining facial data violates the privacy rights of people who may have no knowledge they are being photographed.

cards.headline: Fusion startup Focused Energy raises $240 million
cards.teaser: The company is developing laser-powered fusion technology as an energy source.
cards.body:
Original Card Text

Focused Energy closed a $240 million Series A funding round for its laser-powered fusion technology. The startup is working to develop fusion power as a viable energy source.

The funding represents one of several large investments in fusion startups in recent years. Companies in this sector are attempting to create fusion reactions that generate more energy than they consume, a goal that has remained elusive despite decades of research.

cards.headline: Trump scales back AI oversight order after industry pushback
cards.teaser: The revised executive order makes government reviews of AI models voluntary rather than mandatory.
cards.body:
President Trump signed a revised executive order on artificial intelligence oversight following objections from technology industry representatives. The new order takes a narrower approach than initially proposed, requiring only voluntary prerelease government reviews of advanced AI models.

Under the revised framework, AI companies can voluntarily submit their most powerful models for government testing up to 30 days before public release. However, participation is not mandatory, giving companies the option to opt out of the review process.

cards.headline: OpenAI releases job-specific Codex tools
cards.teaser: The company launched six plugins designed for specific white-collar professions.
cards.body:
OpenAI has launched six new plugins for Codex designed for enterprise users in specific professional roles. The plugins target data analytics, creative production, sales, product design, equity investing, and investment banking. Each tool bundles integrations, instructions, and context to help Codex perform tasks relevant to those fields.

The release reflects OpenAI's effort to expand Codex's applications in workplace settings. The company also published an internal report examining how Codex is currently being used for knowledge work, indicating the tool is finding broader adoption across white-collar professions.

cards.headline: Board raises $20 million for shared-space technology
cards.teaser: The startup from Mirror founder Brynn Putnam has already sold thousands of units.
cards.body:
Board, a startup founded by Brynn Putnam, closed a $20 million Series A funding round led by Union Square Ventures. Putnam previously founded Mirror, a home fitness company.

Board is developing "together tech"—products designed to bring people into the same physical room. The company has already sold thousands of units of its product, marking a shift from remote-focused technology toward tools that facilitate in-person interaction.

cards.headline: Meta tests Series feature for episodic Reels
cards.teaser: The new feature would allow creators to organize short videos into ongoing series on Instagram and Facebook.
cards.body:
Meta is testing a Series feature that organizes Reels into episodic content on Instagram and Facebook. The tool allows creators to build ongoing narratives and recurring themes using short-form video.

Meta is exploring monetization options for Series but has not detailed specific plans. The test reflects Meta's push to compete in the short-form video space and provide creators with additional tools for growing their audiences.

hero.headline: Browns GM says Myles Garrett trade hinged on Rams including Jared Verse
hero.body:
Cleveland Browns general manager Andrew Berry said he would not have seriously pursued trading star defensive end Myles Garrett to the Los Angeles Rams unless the package included edge rusher Jared Verse.

Garrett, a two-time NFL Defensive Player of the Year and seven-time Pro Bowl selection, has been one of the league's most dominant defenders since Cleveland selected him first overall in 2017. He holds the most sacks (125.5), pressures (413) and tackles for loss (149) among all players since that draft. In 2025, he set the single-season sacks record with 23.

The trade sent Garrett to Los Angeles in exchange for Verse, a 2027 first-round selection, a 2028 second-round pick and a 2029 third-round selection. Verse, 25, was a first-round pick by the Rams in 2024 and earned Defensive Rookie of the Year honors. He has recorded 12 career sacks and 22 tackles for loss while earning Pro Bowl selection this past season.

Berry explained the thinking behind the blockbuster deal after it was announced. "As discussions intensified we were stuck at a legitimate crossroads: do we hold on to a truly generational player who has become the identity of our team, or do we make the difficult decision that we think is best for the organization over the long run?" he said.

Garrett had requested a trade from the Browns in 2024 after they finished 3-14, expressing a desire to play for a championship contender. The following month, he signed a four-year, $160 million extension with Cleveland that made him the highest-paid non-quarterback in the league at the time. The deal included $122.8 million guaranteed and an average annual salary of $40 million.

The Browns again missed the playoffs in 2025 with a 5-12 record. Berry was able to facilitate the trade after Garrett and the team agreed to modify his contract in March, deferring option payments over the 2026-28 seasons.

The Rams, fresh off losing in last season's NFC championship game to the eventual Super Bowl champion Seattle Seahawks, are known for aggressive moves. In 2021, they acquired Matthew Stafford from Detroit and won the Super Bowl in his first season with the team.

Garrett's move to Los Angeles reunites him with Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford, who won the AP NFL MVP award last season. This marks the first time a reigning MVP and Defensive Player of the Year will be teammates.

The trade reflects different philosophies for both franchises. The Rams continue their win-now approach by acquiring a proven superstar, while the Browns pivot toward a younger roster build centered around Verse as their defensive anchor for years to come.

cards.headline: Seahawks sign Derick Hall to three-year, $42 million extension
cards.teaser: Seattle locked up edge rusher Derick Hall through 2029 with a deal that includes $21 million guaranteed.
cards.body:
The Seattle Seahawks have agreed to a three-year contract extension with edge rusher Derick Hall worth $42 million through the 2029 season. The deal includes $21 million in guaranteed money, according to Hall's agents.

The extension solidifies Hall's role in Seattle's defensive plans for the coming years as a key contributor to the team's pass rush.

cards.headline: Stephen Curry signs 10-year endorsement deal with Li-Ning
cards.teaser: The NBA star ended his sneaker free agency by agreeing to a decade-long contract with the Chinese athletic apparel company.
cards.body:
Stephen Curry has signed a 10-year endorsement deal with Chinese sportswear company Li-Ning. The agreement marks the end of Curry's free agency in the sneaker market following his split from Under Armour, where he had maintained one of basketball's most prominent signature shoe lines.

The partnership represents a significant move for Li-Ning as it competes with established athletic brands and works to grow its basketball presence. Multiple companies had pursued Curry during his free agency period before he ultimately chose to partner with the Chinese company.

cards.headline: Columbus defenseman Zach Werenski wins Norris Trophy
cards.teaser: The Blue Jackets star was named the NHL's top all-around defenseman for the season.
cards.body:
Zach Werenski of the Columbus Blue Jackets has won the Norris Trophy, awarded annually to the NHL's top all-around defenseman. The honor represents a major career achievement for the Blue Jackets' defensive cornerstone.

The Norris Trophy recognizes excellence across all aspects of defensive play. Werenski's selection underscores his performance this season with Columbus.

cards.headline: Curtis Blair selected to referee NBA Finals for first time
cards.teaser: The referee spent days anxiously checking his email before learning he had been chosen to work the championship series.
cards.body:
Curtis Blair will work the NBA Finals for the first time in his career after being selected by the league for the championship series.

Blair spent days anxiously checking his email as he waited for the NBA to announce its referee assignments. The anticipation lasted through Friday, Saturday, and Sunday before the league finally revealed its selections. Being chosen to officiate the NBA Finals represents a major milestone for referees, who earn the honor based on their performance throughout the season and playoffs.

cards.headline: Browns coach calls drafting Texas Tech QB in supplemental draft a 'slippery slope'
cards.teaser: Todd Monken weighed in on whether Cleveland should pursue Brendan Sorsby if he becomes ineligible for college football.
cards.body:
Cleveland Browns coach Todd Monken said it would be a slippery slope for the team to draft Texas Tech quarterback Brendan Sorsby in the NFL's supplemental draft if he is ruled ineligible to play college football due to his gambling addiction. Monken's comments addressed speculation about whether the Browns might pursue the quarterback through the supplemental draft process.

The supplemental draft allows teams to select players who were not eligible for the regular NFL draft. Sorsby's potential ineligibility stems from issues related to a gambling addiction, which could make him available through this alternative draft mechanism.

cards.headline: Marta Kostyuk advances to French Open semifinals, dedicates win to Ukraine
cards.teaser: The Ukrainian player upset compatriot Elina Svitolina and will face Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva next.
cards.body:
Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk defeated fellow countrywoman Elina Svitolina in a French Open quarterfinal upset, becoming the first woman from her nation to reach the singles semifinals at Roland Garros. Kostyuk dedicated her victory to Ukraine.

She will next face Russian teenager Mirra Andreeva in the semifinals.

hero.headline: Martin Scorsese Joins AI Firm as Adviser, Uses Technology for Film Storyboarding
hero.body:
Director Martin Scorsese has joined artificial intelligence company Black Forest Labs as an adviser and disclosed that he is using AI technology to storyboard his films. The Oscar-winning filmmaker said the partnership aims to push creative boundaries and create deeper experiences for audiences.

Scorsese framed his decision in historical terms, noting that cinema is approximately 125 years old and remains a young medium. He said filmmakers must remain open to how cinema can evolve. The director did not specify which current or upcoming projects involve AI storyboarding tools.

Black Forest Labs is the latest AI company to partner with a major Hollywood figure. The entertainment industry has seen growing adoption of artificial intelligence tools for various production tasks, from script development to visual effects work. Scorsese's involvement represents a significant endorsement from one of cinema's most respected directors.

The filmmaker's embrace of AI technology stands in contrast to concerns raised by some industry professionals about the impact of artificial intelligence on creative jobs. Writers and actors raised AI-related concerns during labor negotiations in recent years, seeking protections around the use of their likenesses and work.

Scorsese has directed films including Taxi Driver, Goodfellas, The Departed, and The Irishman over a career spanning more than five decades. His willingness to adopt new technology follows a pattern of experimentation throughout his career, including early adoption of digital filmmaking techniques. Black Forest Labs has not disclosed the specific AI tools Scorsese is using or how they function in the storyboarding process.

cards.headline: Paramount Lawyer Accuses Some Opponents of Warner Bros. Merger of Antisemitism
cards.teaser: The chief legal counsel for Paramount Skydance said some who oppose the company's pending takeover of Warner Bros. Discovery are motivated by antisemitic views.
cards.body:
Makan Delrahim, chief legal counsel of Paramount Skydance, told the Los Angeles Times that some opponents of the company's pending $111 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery hold antisemitic views. Delrahim described the claims as fear mongering and linked them to prejudice against the deal's leadership.

The Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger led by David Ellison has faced backlash within the entertainment industry. More than a certain number of industry figures have publicly opposed the deal, though Delrahim characterized some of the opposition as rooted in bias rather than legitimate business concerns.

cards.headline: Robert Pattinson Says He Trained Daily for The Batman 2, Reveals 11 Weeks of Night Shoots
cards.teaser: The actor responded to critics of his physique in the first Batman film and disclosed production details for the sequel.
cards.body:
Robert Pattinson told GQ magazine he installed a home gym and worked out every day to build muscle for The Batman: Part II. The actor was responding to viewers who criticized his physical appearance in the 2022 film The Batman. Pattinson used profanity to emphasize his commitment to the training regimen.

Pattinson also revealed that the sequel includes 11 weeks of night shoots. The production schedule suggests extensive outdoor or low-light filming for the superhero film. The Batman: Part II is currently in production, with Pattinson reprising his role as Bruce Wayne.

cards.headline: Boards of Canada Release First Studio Album in 13 Years
cards.teaser: The Scottish electronic duo released Inferno, their first new studio album since 2013.
cards.body:
Scottish electronic production duo Boards of Canada released Inferno, their first studio album in 13 years. The group last released a studio album in 2013, making the new record a long-awaited return for the act known for ambient electronic music.

A review described the album as showcasing limpid lullabies, a style associated with the duo's previous work. Boards of Canada consists of brothers Michael Sandison and Marcus Eoin, who have maintained a low public profile throughout their career while building a dedicated following in electronic music.

cards.headline: Documentary on Cypress Hill Co-Founder Sen Dog Begins Production
cards.teaser: Mi Familia: Sen Dog and the American Dream chronicles the life of Senen Reyes from Cuba to hip-hop stardom.
cards.body:
Production has started on Mi Familia: Sen Dog and the American Dream, a documentary about Cypress Hill co-founder Senen Sen Dog Reyes. The film will trace Reyes' life from his family's origins in Cuba through the streets of South Central Los Angeles to his music career. The documentary will feature appearances by will.i.am, Pitbull, Slash, and other musicians.

The project is described as recounting an untold American Dream story. Cypress Hill became one of the most successful Latin hip-hop groups in music history. Reyes co-founded the group and served as one of its primary vocalists alongside B-Real.

cards.headline: Paul McCartney Album Gets Exclusive White Vinyl Edition
cards.teaser: The Boys of Dungeon Lane is now available on limited white vinyl with a lyric booklet and embossed cover.
cards.body:
Paul McCartney's 20th solo album, The Boys of Dungeon Lane, is available as an exclusive white vinyl edition through Amazon. The release features a 12-page lyric booklet and embossed cover artwork.

McCartney describes the album as "memory songs," reflecting on his extensive career spanning more than six decades. The collector-friendly vinyl format aligns with the current trend of special edition physical releases for major artists.

cards.headline: Dewayne Perkins Develops Dating Comedy Series at Hulu
cards.teaser: The ensemble comedy follows friends in their 30s who make relationship decisions by group vote.
cards.body:
Hulu is developing an untitled ensemble comedy from comedian and actor Dewayne Perkins. The series follows a group of friends in their 30s who practice date by jury, meaning all relationship choices are determined by group vote. The main character is Denny, described as chaotically gay, alongside a straight friend characterized as just trying his best.

Perkins is known for his work in comedy and acting. The project is in

hero.headline: Rubio testifies on U.S. demands in Iran peace talks as conflict worsens
hero.body:
Secretary of State Marco Rubio appeared before the Senate Foreign Relations Committee on Tuesday to detail U.S. demands in ongoing negotiations with Iran, marking his first public testimony since the Trump administration launched the war in February. His appearance comes as Iran has announced it is halting peace talks and moving to fully close the Strait of Hormuz, intensifying the regional conflict.

Rubio claimed that Iran has agreed to negotiate aspects of its nuclear program that officials refused to discuss a month earlier. "There is the prospect before us, which could happen today, it could happen tomorrow, it could happen next week - that for the first time, certainly in my memory, they have agreed to negotiate aspects of their nuclear program that just a month ago they said they would not," he told senators.

The secretary's optimism contrasts sharply with Iran's announcement that it would stop exchanging messages with Washington through intermediaries, citing Israel's military operations in Lebanon as a ceasefire violation. President Trump later insisted that conversations "have been going on continuously" and denied reports that officials had stopped speaking.

Rubio outlined a two-phase framework for negotiations. He stated that reopening the Strait of Hormuz serves as a precondition for talks, not a bargaining chip. Iran must declare it is not charging tolls, assist in removing mines it placed there, and commit not to fire on ships. Only after these conditions are met would phase two discussions begin, which would require Iran to dispose of its highly enriched uranium stockpile and accept "severe and long-term limitations, or cancellation of enrichment activity."

When questioned by Democratic Senator Chris Murphy about offering sanctions relief to reopen the waterway, Rubio ruled out that approach. "Any sanctions relief is condition-based," he said, tied to Iran's nuclear program. "That's not been discussed, that's not been offered."

Regarding Iran's military capabilities, Rubio suggested that the country's missile program has been "substantially degraded" and its drone-building capability "eroded." He claimed there is "no Iranian navy," stating it "lies at the bottom of the ocean." However, he acknowledged that Iran still possesses "a lot of drones" because they are relatively easy to manufacture.

These claims about Iran's military destruction have been contested by independent analysis. The New York Times reported in May that Iran retained roughly 70 percent of its prewar missile stockpile, though over 85 percent of its ballistic missile, drone and naval defense industrial base has been damaged or destroyed.

Rubio noted that a U.S. counter-blockade targeting all ships seeking Iranian ports is costing Tehran "hundreds of millions of dollars a day" in lost oil revenue. This blockade followed Iran's failure to honor an April ceasefire agreement that included a commitment to reopen the strait.

cards.headline: Senate Republicans question Trump pick for national intelligence role
cards.teaser: GOP senators are expressing bewilderment at President Trump's choice of Bill Pulte to serve as acting director of national intelligence.
cards.body:
Republican senators are expressing concern over President Trump's appointment of Bill Pulte as acting director of national intelligence. Pulte, whose family founded PulteGroup, a major homebuilder, currently leads the Federal Housing Finance Agency, which oversees Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. He has no national intelligence experience and limited government background before his FHFA appointment.

Since joining the FHFA, Pulte has made significant changes, including firing board members and appointing himself as chair. His selection as intelligence chief has raised alarm among Washington officials, who question whether a staunch Trump loyalist with his background is qualified to lead the nation's intelligence apparatus.

cards.headline: Trump signs executive order on AI safety with voluntary testing
cards.teaser: President Trump signed an order asking AI companies to voluntarily submit their most powerful models for government review before public release.
cards.body:
President Trump signed an executive order establishing a voluntary AI safety review process. The order asks technology companies to submit their most powerful models to the government for testing up to 30 days before public release.

The voluntary framework reflects the administration's effort to balance AI oversight with industry concerns about innovation. The revised order came after technology companies raised objections to stricter regulatory approaches, resulting in a system that relies on company participation rather than mandatory requirements.

cards.headline: Speaker Johnson says Justice Department fund will be set aside
cards.teaser: House Speaker Mike Johnson announced the Trump administration is abandoning efforts to secure funding for a DOJ program in the pending immigration bill.
cards.body:
Speaker of the House Mike Johnson said a Justice Department fund is being set aside amid confusion among Republicans over spending priorities. Johnson stated the Trump administration is also abandoning efforts to secure funding in the pending party-line immigration bill.

The decision comes as Senate Republicans face obstacles in advancing their spending package. Criticism has mounted over the Justice Department's nearly $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund, which has become a point of contention in GOP reconciliation negotiations.

cards.headline: Homeland Security Secretary Mullin testifies on budget amid GOP spending battle
cards.teaser: Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin appeared before the Senate to discuss the fiscal 2027 budget request.
cards.body:
Secretary Markwayne Mullin testified before the Senate Appropriations Committee regarding President Trump's fiscal 2027 budget request for the Department of Homeland Security. The hearing occurred as Senate Republicans worked to advance a reconciliation bill for DHS funding.

GOP lawmakers faced complications in moving the spending package forward. Speaker Johnson indicated that the Trump administration is abandoning the proposed DOJ anti-weaponization fund and withdrawing efforts to secure ballroom funding in the pending immigration bill.

cards.headline: California governor primary underway with crowded field
cards.teaser: Democrats Katie Porter, Tom Steyer, Xavier Becerra and Republicans Chad Bianco, Steve Hilton compete for nominations to replace Gov. Gavin Newsom.
cards.body:
California voters are deciding which candidates will advance in the governor's race during Tuesday's primary election. Democrats Katie Porter, Tom Steyer, and Xavier Becerra are competing for their party's nomination, while Republicans Chad Bianco and Steve Hilton seek the GOP slot.

The next governor will almost certainly be a Democrat, given California's deep-blue status. Xavier Becerra represents the establishment favorite and has followed a traditional political path, while the race reflects broader questions about what direction the Democratic party will take in overseeing the world's fourth-largest economy.

cards.headline: New Mexico governor primary features Biden administration official
cards.teaser: Sam Bregman, Deb Haaland, Gregg Hull, Duke Rodriguez and Doug Turner compete for nominations to replace Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham.
cards.body:
New Mexico voters are selecting their party nominees for governor in a primary that includes Deb Haaland, who served as an official in the Biden administration. Other candidates in the race include Sam Bregman, Gregg Hull, Duke Rodriguez, and Doug Turner.

The winner will seek to replace Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham. Haaland's presence in the race brings national profile and experience from federal service to the contest for the state's top executive position.
